title: ESA's Rosalind Franklin Rover to Hunt for Ancient Life in Martian Clay at Oxia Planum
summary:
The search for life on Mars is about to get a major boost. The European Space Agency's ExoMars Rosalind Franklin rover, now targeting a 2028 launch, will land at Oxia Planum—a region rich in clay minerals that may hold the best chance yet of finding ancient biosignatures. A new study reveals that these clay deposits extend across 300 kilometers, linking Oxia Planum to Mawrth Vallis and pointing to a vast, water-soaked past.

Clay is a prime target because it forms in the presence of water and can trap organic molecules. 'We will use the instruments on board to ground truth the discoveries made from orbit, learn about the ancient environment in which they formed, and if they preserve any evidence of Martian life,' said deputy project scientist Elliot Sefton-Nash. The rover's drill will penetrate up to two meters below the surface, accessing material shielded from cosmic radiation.

Orbital observations using ESA's OMEGA instrument and NASA's Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter have mapped layered clay deposits and chemical variations that chronicle changing water conditions. Some scientists hypothesize that Oxia Planum once held a vast ocean or experienced cataclysmic flooding around four billion years ago. 'We are targeting the oldest deposits in the sequence, which makes the potential implications for the geology and early climate of Mars very relevant,' said project scientist Jorge Vago.

While previous missions have found tantalizing hints—including what some call the strongest possible biosignature detected last year—Rosalind Franklin will be the first to combine deep drilling with sophisticated onboard analysis. If microbial life ever existed on Mars, its chemical fingerprints may still be locked within that ancient clay. The rover's mission could finally answer the question that has driven decades of exploration: was Mars ever alive?
why_it_matters: The mission tackles one of humanity's oldest questions—are we alone?—with technology that can dig deeper and analyze more precisely than ever before. For a generation growing up with climate change, knowing whether a once-habitable planet lost its life or never had any could offer a sobering lesson about environmental stewardship on Earth.

background_read: The European Space Agency (ESA) is an intergovernmental organization of 22 member states dedicated to space exploration, headquartered in Paris.

The rover is named after Rosalind Franklin, the British chemist whose work on X-ray diffraction helped reveal the structure of DNA—a fitting name for a mission searching for the building blocks of life.

Oxia Planum is one of the largest exposures of clay-bearing rocks on Mars, believed to have formed in water around 3.9 billion years ago, when Mars may have had a thicker atmosphere and flowing rivers.

The ExoMars mission originally included a Russian-built lander, but ESA severed ties with Roscosmos in 2022 due to the war in Ukraine, causing delays and leading to a redesigned landing system now targeting 2028.
NASA's Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter, launched in 2005, has been imaging Mars in high resolution and mapping minerals, providing crucial data for landing site selection.

perspectives.description: If Rosalind Franklin finds clear biosignatures, it would be the most important discovery in the history of science, proving that life is not unique to Earth and opening the door to astrobiology. Even negative results will help refine our understanding of how life emerges and what conditions are needed.

However, the mission has faced multiple delays, ballooning costs, and the loss of its original Russian lander partner, which could jeopardize its timeline or technical success. There is also risk that the rover could contaminate a pristine site with Earth microbes, making it difficult to distinguish Martian life from earthly hitchhikers.

Geologists note that clays can preserve organic matter for billions of years, but the harsh radiation on the Martian surface can break down such molecules over time. The two-meter drill is a compromise—it goes deeper than any previous drill on Mars, but it may still not be deep enough to escape all radiation damage. The choice of Oxia Planum reflects a careful balancing of scientific potential against engineering constraints.

The mission could pave the way for a Mars sample return campaign, where samples collected by Rosalind Franklin and other rovers are eventually brought back to Earth for more detailed analysis. In the longer run, understanding Martian habitability will inform human exploration and the search for life on icy moons like Europa and Enceladus.
